title: Southworth v. Oliver
lead: After approaching a neighbor about selling ranch land, the Olivers sent a letter with acreage, price, and installment terms. Southworth accepted, but the sellers called the material merely informational and insisted the land belonged in a package with grazing permits.

actors.name: Joseph and Arlene Oliver
actors.role: Oregon ranch owners seeking to reduce their operation.

actors.name: Southworth
actors.role: Adjoining cattle rancher who had long wanted the Bear Valley tract.

actors.name: Clyde Holliday
actors.role: Neighbor interested in grazing permits and a possible land exchange.

actors.name: Justice Tongue
actors.role: Author of the Oregon Supreme Court opinion.

proceedings: The trial court ordered specific performance after finding an offer and acceptance. The Oregon Supreme Court affirmed formation and the supplied security terms and rejected a statute-of-frauds defense raised for the first time on appeal.
limits: The statute-of-frauds ruling rests on preservation, not a finding that every signature requirement was met or estoppel established. The court treated security as a subordinate gap in this sufficiently definite bargain. The account uses the reproduced letter’s June 17, 1976 date rather than isolated slips in the report.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Olivers decide to reduce their ranching operation
sections.cue: How did Southworth become the prospective land buyer?
paragraphs: Joseph and Arlene Oliver owned ranches in Oregon’s Bear Valley and John Day valley. In 1976 they and their son decided to sell some Bear Valley land and Forest Service grazing permits. Advice from Joseph’s accountant and attorney led him to require installment payments for income-tax reasons.

Southworth, a cattle rancher with adjoining property, had long wanted the land. On May 20, Joseph approached him about a sale. According to testimony the Supreme Court credited, Joseph suggested Southworth might want the land while neighbor Clyde Holliday might want the grazing permits. They identified the tract on a map but did not settle price or payment terms. Joseph would determine value and price; Southworth would investigate financing.

Joseph later emphasized giving neighbors information and a first opportunity, though he acknowledged the mapped tract was the one ultimately presented to four neighbors. Nobody discussed requiring Southworth to buy permits with the land. Southworth spoke with Holliday, who expressed interest in permits and a possible exchange, rather than buying the tract himself.

sections.title: The June letter supplies price and payment terms for the mapped tract
paragraphs: On June 13, Southworth called to confirm the sale plans. Joseph said they continued and that he awaited the assessor’s information. Southworth reported that his financing was ready.

Arlene prepared a June 17 letter and enclosures after discussions with Joseph, who read and signed it. The letter described information about previously discussed ranch sales, said prices reflected the assessor’s market valuations, and invited questions. One enclosure identified about 2,933 acres near Seneca: $306,409 for land and $18,010 for improvements, totaling $324,419. Terms were twenty-nine percent down and the balance over five years at eight percent interest. The sale date would be negotiated for December 1, 1976, or January 1, 1977, with availability following hay harvest and arrangements to remove hay, equipment, and supplies.

Two grazing permits were separately listed, and another enclosure concerned roughly 6,365 acres near John Day. Joseph mailed the materials to Southworth, Holliday, and two other neighbors. He later testified that he intended more negotiations and a combined land-and-permits transfer. That asserted intent differed from what the trial court found his words and conduct objectively conveyed.

sections.title: Southworth accepts before the sellers deny making a firm offer
sections.cue: Why did the controversy lead to specific performance?
paragraphs: Southworth wrote June 21 accepting the Bear Valley land offer. After Holliday reported difficulty arranging an exchange with Southworth, Joseph said he did not want to arbitrate neighbors’ disagreements and might withdraw the property.

The Olivers’ June 24 letter denied any firm offer, insisted that land and permits were not separately available, questioned the legal description, and invited further negotiation. Southworth sought a declaration that they were bound to sell. After trial, the court entered a specific-performance decree. The Olivers appealed on offer, acceptance, and definiteness and added a general demurrer in the Supreme Court invoking the statute of frauds.

sections.title: The letter completes the negotiations rather than merely beginning them
sections.cue: Why did its informational label not control?
paragraphs: Justice Tongue wrote for the five participating Justices. The inquiry was what a reasonable person in Southworth’s position would understand from the whole setting, not undisclosed intent. A price quotation alone ordinarily invited negotiation, but surrounding circumstances could make it a commitment completed by assent. Language, identified rather than indefinite recipients, and definiteness all informed that objective question. Mailing to several people was relevant, not categorically fatal.

Joseph had solicited Southworth, identified the tract, undertaken to determine price, and heard that financing would be and then was arranged. The letter supplied that price and definite installment terms. It went to four identified neighbors, not an indefinite public. Its references to information and selling, and omission of the word offer, did not outweigh those dealings. A reasonable recipient could understand an offer.

sections.title: The land-only reply accepts an objectively separate offer
sections.cue: Why did permit-transfer restrictions not establish an inseparable package?
paragraphs: The Olivers argued that grazing permits required commensurate land or cattle for transfer and that they did not want to sell cattle. They treated Southworth’s response as a counteroffer omitting an essential component.

The trial court had found both that negotiations permitted a separate land sale and that permit terms were too indefinite for a firm offer. Those were independent grounds; the Supreme Court did not need to approve every aspect of the latter.

The decisive prior discussion contemplated Holliday taking permits and Southworth the land. A neighbor might arrange supporting land, or the sellers might retain permits backed by remaining land or cattle. Southworth therefore could reasonably read the land as separately available. Any tension between definite land terms and indefinite permit terms did not defeat that ground. His land-only acceptance matched the offer instead of selecting part of an inseparable bargain.

sections.title: Equity supplies customary security details within the agreed installment sale
sections.cue: Why was the omitted security device not fatal?
paragraphs: The sellers argued that failure to select security made the bargain too indefinite. The Court distinguished a prior case lacking agreement about conveyance or an entitlement to compel installments, where the buyer could pay cash instead. Here the parties expressly chose a down payment and five years of installments. Southworth had no right to substitute full cash, and the sellers agreed to defer payment.

Within reasonable limits, equity could settle subordinate details after sufficient manifested intent to contract. The omitted security terms fit that category, and concern over them had not prompted the attempted withdrawal.

The decree used a standard printed installment land-sale contract with customary provisions for repairs and insurance, taxes and liens, default remedies, time of the essence, and nonwaiver. It did not adopt the note-and-mortgage device from the analogous precedent. Upholding these supplied details did not give courts general authority to invent missing essential bargains.

sections.title: A new statute-of-frauds objection arrives too late
sections.cue: What did the Court decline to decide about signatures and authorization?
paragraphs: The appellate demurrer asserted that Joseph had not subscribed the agreement, Arlene had not signed, and the complaint lacked an allegation of Joseph’s written authority to bind her. The sellers invoked a precedent permitting a failure-to-state-a-claim objection at any time, but there the demurrer had actually been raised and rejected below.

The statute-of-frauds defense could be waived. A timely objection could permit pleading and proof overcoming it. Because the Olivers had raised no such objection in the trial court, they could not introduce it on appeal through demurrer or otherwise.

Arlene had drafted the letter, Joseph signed as Joe, and both signed the later denial without disavowing joint authorization of the first communication. Southworth also incurred litigation expense in reliance on the offer. Those circumstances might support ratification, waiver, or estoppel, but the Court expressly did not decide their sufficiency. Preservation resolved the issue.

sections.title: The land-sale decree is affirmed
paragraphs: The Oregon Supreme Court affirmed the decree requiring Joseph and Arlene Oliver to sell Southworth the approximately 2,933-acre tract. The result followed a completed trial and established offer, acceptance, and sufficient certainty, not merely an adequate pleading. No separate opinion was reported.

The rejected statute-of-frauds objection did not establish that an unsigned spouse’s agreement necessarily satisfies the statute. The decree stood because the defense had not been raised when it could have been litigated below.
